description: Blending the power of science with space technologies, Astraxis sets out to create innovative and sustainable solutions for humanity.
summary: Lunaris is a prototype mission-planning tool for the preliminary assessment of lunar south-pole landing locations. It combines NASA’s LRO LOLA elevation data with SPICE/Skyfield ephemerides to examine how local terrain affects Sun illumination and direct-to-Earth visibility. For a selected site and UTC epoch, its analysis backend is designed to calculate a 360° terrain horizon, estimate terrain-aware sunlight duration, evaluate Earth line of sight, and derive local slope, roughness, and a Landing Suitability Index. Lunaris also compares representative points from nine Artemis III candidate regions over a shared mission interval and provides annual and 18.6-year illumination pre-screens for potential permanently shadowed regions. By bringing terrain, illumination, and visibility indicators into one workflow, it supports clearer early-stage site exploration. Lunaris is a decision-support prototype, not a landing-safety certification: the 40 m/pixel DEM cannot resolve small surface hazards, and its outputs do not constitute power-generation or full communications-link simulations.
details: LUNARIS is a project focused on one of the most challenging parts of future lunar exploration: finding suitable landing locations near the Moon’s south pole. When we first started working on this idea, we wanted to go beyond simply displaying the lunar surface in 3D. We wanted to build something that could help people understand what makes a landing site suitable, what problems a mission might face there, and how conditions on the Moon can change over time. To do this, LUNARIS uses real elevation data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), collected by the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA). This data allows us to create a 3D representation of the lunar south pole and examine its terrain. The platform looks at several factors that could affect a landing mission, including slope, surface roughness, the surrounding horizon, sunlight availability, and visibility between a location and Earth. We chose to consider these factors together because a relatively flat location may still be difficult to use if nearby terrain blocks sunlight or prevents communication with Earth. An important part of the project is understanding how the Sun and Earth appear from different points on the lunar surface. Using NASA SPICE kernels and astronomical calculations, LUNARIS estimates when these objects are visible from selected locations. This is especially relevant at the lunar south pole, where sunlight conditions can be very different from what we experience on Earth. The platform also compares representative Artemis III candidate landing regions and calculates a Landing Suitability Index using terrain characteristics such as slope and roughness. We also considered longer lunar orbital cycles, including the draconic year and the 18.6-year nodal cycle, to explore how illumination conditions may change over time. We wanted LUNARIS to bring these different types of information into one place rather than make users examine separate datasets and tools. Through its interactive 3D environment, users can explore the terrain, examine mission-related conditions, and compare different locations. Our goal is to make this kind of information easier to understand and to show that choosing a lunar landing site involves much more than finding a flat area. We hope the project can be useful for educational purposes and provide an accessible starting point for people interested in lunar exploration and mission planning. Most of the project was developed using Python. FastAPI handles the backend, while NumPy, Rasterio, Plotly, SpiceyPy, Skyfield, and Pydantic support numerical calculations, terrain processing, astronomical analysis, and data management. The interactive interface is built with HTML and JavaScript, allowing users to explore the results in a web browser. NASA LRO LOLA elevation data and NASA SPICE resources are at the core of the scientific side of the project. We also used Docker to package the application and GitHub to manage the source code and development process. Since LUNARIS is a software-based platform, it does not require dedicated physical hardware. Building LUNARIS also involved working through some practical challenges. Processing large terrain datasets, handling astronomical data, connecting the calculations to the backend, and presenting the results in an interactive 3D interface required different parts of the system to work together. We had to think not only about the calculations themselves, but also about how someone using the platform would understand the results. This influenced many of our development decisions. LUNARIS is still an early-stage analysis and decision-support project, not a certified system for determining landing safety. The resolution of the available elevation data limits how much small-scale surface detail can be examined, and the Landing Suitability Index is a preliminary assessment rather than a validated mission standard. We believe it is important to be clear about these limitations. Our aim is not to replace professional mission-planning systems, but to demonstrate how publicly available NASA data, scientific calculations, and interactive software can be combined to explore real challenges in future lunar missions. Ultimately, we hope LUNARIS makes the lunar south pole a little easier to explore, understand, and imagine as a destination for future human exploration.
